title: A Public LBO
coreMove: Make a public company answer owner-like economic tests by forcing sprawl, side bets, and operating softness to justify their capital.
sourcePressure: Bill Stiritz and Ralston Purina show public-market management run with private-owner discipline, pruning unrelated operations and tightening focus around sharper economics.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Do not write PE worship or generic austerity; show public-company sprawl being forced through an owner-like scorecard with operating rigor after the pruning.

sourceAnchors.name: Bill Stiritz
sourceAnchors.detail: The source sidecar pairs Chapter 6 with Bill Stiritz and Ralston Purina and says he created private-equity-like economics inside a public company.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Bill Stiritz makes public ownership feel less like a permission slip for softness and more like a place to impose owner standards.

sourceAnchors.name: Ralston Purina
sourceAnchors.detail: The source sidecar says Ralston Purina had accumulated unrelated businesses and that Stiritz tightened focus by selling operations that did not fit the core.
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Ralston Purina gives the public LBO idea its bite because sprawl had to stop receiving automatic subsidy.

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: No more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'.
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: At least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person direct address, retrospective, question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human.
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

exampleSpecs.domain: publicly funded housing nonprofit with unrelated pilot programs
exampleSpecs.audience: an executive director accountable to a broad board and city funders
exampleSpecs.stakes: core repair backlog growing while pilots absorb grant staff
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Michael pins each pilot to a repair-backlog dollar and closes the popular rooftop-garden expansion because it does not strengthen the core housing economics.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a cracked window work order under a city grant folder

exampleSpecs.domain: listed specialty food company deciding whether to sell a pet-snack sideline
exampleSpecs.audience: a CFO whose board likes the appearance of category breadth
exampleSpecs.stakes: cash trapped in the sideline could fund automation in the profitable sauce plant
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Catarina walks from the pet-snack inventory racks to the sauce bottling line and marks which asset earns automation capital under the owner scorecard.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: sealed pet-snack cartons stacked beside a sauce-line repair tag

exampleSpecs.domain: software company after years of buying small tools that never integrate
exampleSpecs.audience: a public-company product chief with six underused acquisitions
exampleSpecs.stakes: engineering attention split while the flagship product misses enterprise renewals
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Sam asks which acquired tool changes renewal economics, sunsets two vanity acquisitions, and moves engineers back to the core platform reliability work.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: an integration dashboard with six red warning triangles

exampleSpecs.domain: regional fitness chain pruning boutique class brands after expansion
exampleSpecs.audience: an operations VP facing franchisees who like the wider menu
exampleSpecs.stakes: trainer utilization and equipment maintenance are weakening the core gym model
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: After three utilization audits, Anke closes two low-return class brands and installs a stricter weekly operating dashboard for the core gyms.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: unused reformer machines lined against a studio mirror

exampleSpecs.domain: airport services contractor reviewing lounge, cleaning, and baggage add-ons
exampleSpecs.audience: a division manager whose public parent company rewards revenue breadth
exampleSpecs.stakes: margin leakage in side contracts threatens the core baggage-handling renewal
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: You expect the newest lounge contract to be the growth engine; Pablo reveals the working-capital schedule and cuts it because the core baggage renewal has better owner economics.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a baggage tug parked below a lounge-service invoice

exampleSpecs.domain: regional veterinary group centralizing procurement after scattered clinic acquisitions
exampleSpecs.audience: a CEO who wants scale benefits without smothering clinic medicine
exampleSpecs.stakes: drug costs and local autonomy both at risk after acquisitions
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: What would an owner keep strict and what would she leave local? Hannah centralizes supplier terms and kills weak side ventures while leaving medical protocols with clinic leads.
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a vaccine refrigerator temperature strip beside a supplier rebate sheet

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm: a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'

skillTargets: identify public-company softness hiding in sprawl
choose pruning that clarifies economics rather than merely shrinking
test whether operating rigor follows portfolio action
separate owner-like standards from harsh style

tryThisNowSpec: Pick one active side bet and write the core economic measure it must improve; if it cannot improve that measure, write the first resource you would stop feeding it.
